title: POC Weekly Sync - Onboarding & Env Readiness
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on onboarding progress, access (VPC peering + IAM), and initial benchmark results. Redwood reviewed latency and cost numbers from last run, recommended quantization + batching tweaks. Customer agreed to provide VPC CIDR and test account; Redwood to send updated benchmark sheet and SOC2 link. Next meeting to review tuned results after latency test and VPC peering is set up.
topics: Access: VPC peering, service account, KMS
next_steps: Redwood to send updated benchmarking spreadsheet and cost estimates
Brightlane to provide VPC CIDR and AWS account ID for peering
Schedule on-prem install deep-dive if required after peering
Run latency test with provided account and share logs
action_items: Dylan Park - Share benchmark spreadsheet and updated cost scenarios - 2026-09-11
Tom Wu - Provide VPC CIDR, AWS account ID, and confirm security group rules - 2026-09-10
Maya Singh - Run 2k token concurrency latency test and upload logs to shared folder - 2026-09-14
transcript:
[00:00] Dylan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for 45 minutes, agenda is quick onboarding check, access and peering, then the benchmark results we ran last night, and actions.
[00:15] Raj (Brightlane CTO): Yeah, thanks. Busy week but we made time.
[00:20] Elena (ML Eng): Hi all. I have the test artifacts open.
[00:25] Maya (Redwood SE): Hi, Maya here. Quick note, I'll jump into the logs and explain the numbers later.
[00:30] Tom (DevOps): Tom on my side. I have notes on VPC peering and IAM.
[00:37] Dylan: Great. Quick status — onboarding checklist: service account created? Tom?
[00:44] Tom: We created the cross-account role yesterday, but we haven't given the Redwood service account access to the S3 bucket for model inputs. We'll need a policy and the account ID.
[00:55] Dylan: Cool, I'll send the exact policy snippet. Also need the VPC CIDR for peering and the AWS account ID — that was in the onboarding doc.
[01:05] Raj: Right, we'll provide that today. Question on encryption — do you require KMS keys or can we use our default?
[01:12] Maya: For the POC hosted test we can use Redwood-managed KMS, but for Private/VPC tests we recommend customer-managed KMS to match your compliance posture. It's a small config change.
[01:24] Sofia (Product): Is SOC2 paperwork available? Security wants to see it before we open peering.
[01:30] Dylan: Yes, I'll share the SOC2 link and summary in the follow-up email.
[01:36] Elena: On the benchmark, quick context: we ran three workloads — short chat (<= 128 tokens), medium summarization (~512 tokens), and long generation (~2k tokens).
[01:48] Maya: I'll walk through the numbers — keep in mind the infra was Redwood-hosted for this run, not Dedicated. So latency includes our fronting layer.
[01:58] [02:00] Maya: For short chat 95th p99 was ~120 ms per token, median ~70 ms. For medium summarization p95 ~220 ms, p99 ~310 ms. Long generation had steady throughput about 18 tokens/sec on the test V100-ish instance; average latency per token depends on batching.
[02:25] Raj: 120 ms p99 per token — that seems optimistic. Are these end-to-end numbers including network to our region?
[02:33] Maya: These are from the Redwood region us-west-2; your app running elsewhere will add to that. For your internal calc, add ~30-60ms depending on peering and routing.
[02:44] Tom: On our side, we saw some spikes when concurrency hit ~200 simultaneous requests. Any recommendations?
[02:52] Maya: Yes — two levers: increase per-request batching and enable KV caching for repeated prefixes. Because your use case has a lot of repeated prompt fragments, KV cache reduced token compute by about 18% in our internal repro.
[03:06] Elena: KV cache is that the key-value cache for the transformer KVs?
[03:10] Maya: Yep — sometimes transcribed as KV cash in docs — but it's KV cache stored in memory on the serving nodes to avoid recomputing prefixes.
[03:20] Dylan: Also we recommended a 4-bit quantized model for Dedicated to save cost. Did you test quantized?
[03:26] Elena: We tried q4 on a small sample; quality drop was visible on some hallucination-prone prompts.
[03:32] Maya: Right, quantization tradeoff depends on your tolerance. For retrieval-augmented generation we often recommend q4 with a small calibration set and QA checks; otherwise q8 or fp16. We can run a calibration job on your eval set.
[03:46] [04:00] Dylan: Let's step through the actual test artifacts — Elena, can you confirm you uploaded the test prompts to the shared folder?
[04:07] Elena: Yes, all prompts and eval metrics are in the folder under /brightlane/poc/benchmarks. There's a CSV with latency by request ID.
[04:15] Maya: I pulled that and correlated with our logs. There's a mismatch for 12 requests where tokenization probably differed — we saw off-by-one token counts. That can skew latency a bit.
[04:27] Raj: Hmm, we use a custom tokenizer in production; should we align with Redwood's tokenizer?
[04:33] Maya: Ideally yes, at least for consistent evaluation. We can add your tokenizer spec to the job and rerun.
[04:40] Tom: On peering, our security needs to lock source ports and SG rules. Is there a minimal set of ports/protocols?
[04:47] Maya: For the VPC peering with Private deployment it's just HTTPS outbound to Redwood's serving subnets; we support mTLS if you want. If you're doing Dedicated with private network we can give you a narrow IP range for the nodes.
[05:00] Dylan: I'll attach the network checklist in the follow-up.
[05:05] Sofia: About costs — you mentioned cost per 1k tokens last week. Can we get specific numbers for q4 vs fp16?
[05:12] Dylan: Yes — in the updated spreadsheet I'll include per-token and per-minute estimates across configurations (hosted vs dedicated vs private). For example, ballpark: fp16 hosted was ~$0.60 per 1k tokens for this model, q4 could be ~40% lower, but those are rough. We'll put concrete numbers after we validate quality tradeoffs.
[05:32] Raj: That's helpful. Also timeline: our execs want a recommended config by end of next week. Is that possible?
[05:39] Maya: If you provide the VPC details and we run the calibration and concurrency test this week, we can deliver a recommendation by next Friday.
[05:46] Elena: One note on concurrency testing — we want the test to mirror our peak: about 350 concurrent active users, typical message length 300 tokens.
[05:55] Maya: Got it — we'll run a synthetic load with 350 concurrency and 300 token average. We'll also test a burst scenario up to 800 for 2 minutes.
[06:06] Tom: For the peering process, do you prefer we create a role and share the role ARN, or do you need a cross-account link?
[06:13] Dylan: Cross-account role ARN is fine; for peering we just need the account ID and CIDR and we'll send the peering request from our side.
[06:20] Tom: We'll get that today.
[06:22] [06:30] Raj: Anything blocking us from moving to the next phase?
[06:33] Dylan: Not really — network and the S3 permissions are the last blockers. Once Tom confirms the policy and peering we can spin up a private test environment that mirrors your prod VPC.
[06:45] Elena: On logs — what format will you need for debugging? We can ship JSON lines with request_id, prompt, token_count, and latency_ms.
[06:53] Maya: That's perfect. Include the model version you used and the tokenizer.
[06:57] Dylan: Quick question — for audit logging and retention, does Brightlane have a retention period requirement?
[07:03] Raj: We need 7 years for certain logs for compliance, but for POC we can start with 90 days and discuss retention in the enterprise contract.
[07:12] Maya: We can set retention policies per customer — will note that for the enterprise review.
[07:18] Sofia: If we decide to go Dedicated later, how disruptive is the migration?
[07:23] Maya: Minimal from an API perspective — same endpoints, same SDK. There's work on model pinning and routing, but we support canary rollouts, so cutover is manageable.
[07:33] Dylan: Ok let's capture immediate next steps — Tom to provide VPC info and S3 policy; Dylan to share SOC2 + benchmark sheet; Maya to run concurrency and calibration tests once peering is set.
[07:47] Raj: Sounds good. One small item — can you also include an example IAM policy snippet?
[07:53] Dylan: Yup, I'll include a snippet and a sample trust policy.
[07:56] [08:00] Maya: One last thing on tuning: enable continuous batching at 50 ms aggregation window for your workload; it tends to reduce p99 by 12-15% with small impact on median. We'll include recommended settings in the sheet.
[08:12] Elena: Great. Also can you annotate the eval CSV with notes about which prompts are most sensitive to quantization?
[08:19] Maya: We'll add a column with a qualitative score from our calibration run.
[08:23] Dylan: Perfect. Any other questions?
[08:26] Tom: None from infra side.
[08:28] Raj: All good.
[08:30] Dylan: Okay wrapping up — we'll send the follow-up with attachments and action items. Next sync same time next week unless we need to move it.
[08:38] Sofia: Thanks everyone.
[08:40] Elena: Thanks.
[08:41] Maya: Thanks, bye.
[08:43] Dylan: Bye.
[08:45] [END]
